overview: Segu was a powerful Bamana kingdom along the Niger in present-day Mali. Its armies, farmers, boat operators and artists made the river towns a major regional centre. Royal wealth also depended on warfare and the enslavement of captives.

periods.title: Building a river kingdom
periods.summary: Biton Kulibali transformed a youth association into a permanent military force during the early eighteenth century.

periods.title: Diarra rulers and conquest
periods.summary: Ngolo Diarra established a new ruling dynasty later in the eighteenth century. Umar Tal conquered Segu in 1861.

items.text: Biton Kulibali built his power through the tonjonw, an association that became a standing army. Raids supplied captives, some forced into military service and others sold to obtain horses, weapons and luxury goods.

Mungo Park reached Segu in July 1796 and described four walled towns on both banks of the Niger. He saw flat-roofed clay houses, some two storeys high and whitewashed, alongside mosques. The capital was a cluster of settlements connected by water.

Park recorded a fare of ten cowrie shells for a river crossing. The ferries were worked by enslaved people for the king. Some boats joined two hollowed trunks end to end and could carry horses as well as passengers: this was a serious transport service.

When Park was stranded outside the town, a woman returning from field work offered shelter. Her household supplied a mat, a lamp and fish cooked over embers. This encounter in a traveller’s diary preserves a family’s generosity across a language barrier.

After the meal, the women in that household spun cotton and sang through part of the night. Park’s account catches work and social life happening together. Cloth did not begin in a shop: somebody first had to turn fibre into thread.

The Met’s account of Bamana village life describes extended families cultivating fields, with outlying plots demanding seasonal labour at planting and harvest. Farming supported the social world celebrated in sculpture, even though kings and battles occupy more space in written histories.

Bamana society also included specialist craft groups and enslaved people. A beautiful carved object belonged to a society with unequal ranks and demanding labour. Appreciating the maker’s skill should include remembering the different circumstances of the people who produced food, cloth and tools.

A surviving Ci Wara headdress combines features associated with an antelope and other burrowing animals. In performance, paired dancers wore carved headdresses and raffia while women sang encouragement. The spectacle celebrated agricultural skill: farming could have its own cheering section.

The story of Ci Wara tells of a partly human, partly animal being who taught cultivation. This is a sacred origin story, not an archaeological account of agriculture’s invention. The museum’s nineteenth to early twentieth century carving shows how that story took visible form.

A Bamana mother-and-child figure at the University of Michigan dates to the late nineteenth or early twentieth century. Its subject foregrounds motherhood and the continuation of a community across generations. It belongs to the cultural world that continued after the kingdom’s conquest.

A later Bamana power object, or boli, in the Met contains wood, cloth and accumulated organic materials. Offerings changed its surface over time. Its lumpy outline records repeated acts of care and ritual, rather than a sculptor aiming for a neatly polished finish.

Try a short greeting in modern written Bambara: “I ni sɔgɔma”, meaning “Good morning”. The Peace Corps lesson prints this in today’s Latin alphabet. It introduces the continuing language; it is not presented as the spelling on an eighteenth-century royal document.

ending.text: Umar Tal conquered Segu in 1861. The Bamana kingdom lost its independence, while its people, farming traditions and artistic practices continued under changing governments. The map record’s 1815 cutoff precedes this conquest.
